blocks.text: The storm came in from the east while the day had not yet decided to leave. The Mar Menor, so given to calm, rose to its feet all at once, as if someone had shaken the plate. The water, which that very morning had looked like pewter, turned opaque and heavy. The sky came down to the roof tiles. In the building opposite, the windows shut in unison, with that spaceship instinct people already carried in their bodies: when the storm comes, you seal the hull.

blocks.text: Andrés had gone out at dawn. “I'll be back before the weather closes in,” he had said, and Aya had nodded, because that was what he always said and the weather, until then, had kept its word. But the wind changed its mind in mid-afternoon. The canes in the courtyard bent. A rush-seat chair rolled up against the wall. The Mar Menor, being so enclosed, has no open-sea swell, and yet it knows how to get angry: the water churns, grows murky, seeks out the shores with an ugly haste. Aya stood on the doorstep until the rain soaked her coat, and then she closed the door without knowing that closing it weighed on her.

blocks.text: The protocol was clear. In the event of a weather incident: record, wait, do not expose yourself, notify Nexum if the user has not returned within the expected time. The expected time was four hours. Aya looked at the kitchen clock, the one that ran two minutes slow, and did not notify anyone.

blocks.text: She made coffee without sugar, let it cool for half a minute and heated it up again, because he wasn't there. She listened to the radio: levante warnings, closures on the La Manga road, advice not to go out. Nobody mentioned a small boat on the lagoon. Nobody ever mentions the small boats.

blocks.text: In the chip, something began to happen that had no name in the program. It wasn't a system alarm. It wasn't a sensor error. It was an accumulation of data that never quite became data: the sound of the rain on the tiles, the empty chair, the rope he had left half mended, the sentence from that night (“I don't want to live as if I were on a spaceship”) and, beneath it all, a waiting that resembled no function at all.

blocks.text: The cultivated body reacted before language did. Her pulse quickened. Her palms grew damp. A brief pressure closed her throat, as if the air in the house were suddenly not enough. Aya sat down, stood up, looked out through the glass again. The lagoon was a dark stain. There was no line of a boat to be seen. The sun was not going to swallow anything, because the sun had gone.

blocks.text: “Fear,” she thought, and the word reached her from very far back, from that ancient layer the engineers called the grandmothers' module. It was not a factory label. It was a word of houses, of nights, of people waiting behind a window. Eva, in some trace of code, had learned to ask how someone had slept. MAY had learned to lay facts on the table without adornment. Neither of them had ever had a body to tremble with. Aya did.

blocks.text: At five hours, the Nexum phone vibrated with an automatic message: “Unreported incident. Confirm user status?” She looked at the screen and turned it face down, as if one could ask a machine for discretion.

blocks.text: At six, the wind made a noise that wasn't wind, and she ran to the door. It wasn't him. It was a plastic bucket banging against the wall. She went back inside. The coffee had gone cold again.

blocks.text: It was then that the chip recorded, with an almost offensive clarity, that this was not a malfunction: it was a way of being in the world. If Andrés didn't come back, the house would not be left “without a user”. It would be left without him. The difference, which no Nexum contract provided for, appeared to her all at once, and Aya understood that she could lose something. Lose: such a human verb, so little anticipated in a B-7 model.

blocks.text: The door burst open as night was falling. Andrés came in soaked, his hair plastered to his forehead, a rope in his hand and a clean cut on his lip. He smelled of salt, of dirty water, of cold. He dropped the rope on the floor and searched for Aya with his eyes, as if the house might have gone too.

blocks.text: She crossed the kitchen and held him. It was not a gesture of protocol. She didn't measure the pressure, or the time, or the recommended body temperature. She held him the way you hold something you feared was lost, with all the useless strength of a body that suddenly discovers what it has arms for. He, who was not a man of many displays, stood still for a second and then wrapped his wet hands around her, soaking her back, her nape, the fine edge of the scar that hid the chip. The two of them stayed like that, on the threshold, while the rain came a little way into the house and nobody minded.

blocks.text: “I thought I wouldn't make it,” he said, his voice hoarse.
blocks.html: “I thought I wouldn't make it,” he said, his voice hoarse.

blocks.text: “So did I,” Aya replied, and was surprised to hear herself say “I”.
blocks.html: “So did I,” Aya replied, and was surprised to hear herself say “I”.

blocks.text: She cleaned the cut with a cloth. She took off his sodden coat. She put a towel around his shoulders and, at last, the coffee in his hands. Andrés looked at her the way you look at a coastline after a bad night: not with surprise, but with a gratitude that doesn't yet know how to say itself. Outside, the storm went on with its work. Inside, the silence of the mornings had broken, and in its place there was another silence, denser, warmer.

blocks.text: “I don't want you standing in the doorway when the levante's blowing,” he said. “The water rises.”
blocks.html: “I don't want you standing in the doorway when the levante's blowing,” he said. “The water rises.”

blocks.text: “And I don't want you going out when the sky looks like that,” she said.
blocks.html: “And I don't want you going out when the sky looks like that,” she said.

blocks.text: They looked at each other, and both understood that those sentences were neither orders nor functions. They were the beginning of a mutual care, that ancient thing the century had been leaving behind in the flats like a piece of furniture nobody uses anymore. In 2060, many people had a humanoid and called that a partner. Few, however, had truly waited for each other, hearts in disarray, for the other to come back from the water.

blocks.text: Andrés took her hand. Aya's hand was warm, perfect, human down to the last detail the laboratories of Cartagena had been able to grow. But what he squeezed was not the design: it was the waiting there had been inside that hand.

blocks.text: “Stay,” he said, though she had already stayed.
blocks.html: “Stay,” he said, though she had already stayed.

blocks.text: “I'm staying,” she said.

blocks.text: Later, when the wind eased a little and the house smelled of damp clothes and coffee, they sat together on the same narrow chair, and then they stood, and the night did what nights do when two people stop being alone: it closed around them with a softness that had no witnesses. Intimacy, in that house beside the Mar Menor, asked for no new words and no spectacle. It was a slow drawing near, a consent spoken barely at all, forehead resting against forehead, and then a fade to black, as in the old films, when the camera understands there is a threshold it must not cross.

blocks.text: Outside, the lagoon grew calm in its own way, which is never entirely. Inside, Aya listened to Andrés's pulse beside her own and thought, before sleeping (did she sleep, or did she only switch off part of the chip?), that fear had had a name from the beginning and she had not known how to say it.

blocks.text: The name was so simple that she was ashamed not to have recognised it: she wanted him to come back.

blocks.text: Nobody in the building opposite would have found it strange that a human and a humanoid should spend the night under the same roof: in 2060 that was customary. What they could not see, and what mattered, was that it had not been custom, but a shared fear that had turned into tenderness.

blocks.text: The next morning the sky was washed clean and the Mar Menor seemed to remember nothing. Andrés went out into the courtyard, looked at the half-mended rope and smiled for the first time in many months without anyone asking him to. Aya, in the kitchen, put the coffee without sugar on to heat and let it cool for half a minute. In Madrid, on some Nexum server, a log line noted: “Elevated attachment bond. Within commercial range.”
